name: osquery
vendor: osquery project (Linux Foundation), started at Facebook

foundation.via: Moved from Facebook in 2019; run by a Technical Steering Committee from several companies

summary: An agent for Linux, macOS and Windows that exposes the operating system as SQL tables, so you can query processes, users, open ports, installed software and more, interactively or on a schedule that logs what changed.
intro: osquery turns a machine’s state into roughly 290 virtual tables: `processes`, `users`, `listening_ports`, `kernel_modules`, browser extensions, installed packages, certificates, file hashes and many platform-specific ones. Its SQL is a superset of SQLite’s, so you can filter and `JOIN` tables, such as listening ports to the processes that own them; it is `SELECT` only, and `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` do nothing unless an extension supports them. `osqueryi` is an interactive shell for exploring one machine or investigating an incident. `osqueryd` is the daemon you deploy to a fleet: it runs scheduled queries, each with an `interval` in seconds, and logs only the differences since the last run as rows `added` or `removed`, or a full snapshot if you ask for one.

Most tables read the current state when queried, but evented tables keep a buffer of events between runs: `process_events` and `socket_events` from the Linux Audit system, `bpf_process_events` from eBPF on kernel 4.18 and newer, and `es_process_events` from Apple’s EndpointSecurity framework. Results go to logger plugins, including files, syslog, the Windows Event Log, a TLS endpoint, Kafka and Amazon Kinesis or Firehose, and from there into a SIEM where detection rules run. A watchdog stops queries that use too much CPU or memory and denylists them for a day. Tables can be added through a Thrift-based extensions API. The project is dual-licensed under Apache 2.0 and GPL 2.0, and 5.24.0 came out on October 9, 2026.
strengths: One query language for three operating systems: the same SQL asks about processes, users or ports on Linux, macOS and Windows
Differential logging keeps output small: a scheduled query emits only rows that appeared or disappeared since its last run
Broad and growing coverage, from kernel modules to browser and editor extensions; an `ai_agent_skills` table listing coding agents’ installed `SKILL.md` packages was added in October 2026
Vendor-neutral: no single company controls it since Facebook handed it to the Linux Foundation, whose osquery effort was formed with Facebook, Google, Kolide, Trail of Bits, Uptycs and Dactiv
limits: It collects data; it does not alert, block or correlate. Detection rules, dashboards and response live in the SIEM or management server that receives its logs
Managing thousands of agents needs a separate server for remote configuration and log collection, through the TLS plugins or a commercial product
Evented tables are off by default and depend on platform mechanisms with their own flags and costs, such as Linux Audit, eBPF or macOS EndpointSecurity
Point-in-time tables only see what exists when the query runs, so a short-lived process between two scheduled runs is missed unless an evented table catches it

story: Facebook developed osquery in 2014 as a tool that makes it easier to collect low-level system information and spot potential security issues, built around one idea: present the operating system as a high-performance relational database, so that anyone can investigate a machine by writing SQL.

By 2019 the project had, in Trail of Bits’ words, “outgrown its original home as a Facebook project”: about 35 pull requests had been merged in nine months, few from outside Facebook, a move to Facebook’s Buck build system troubled outside contributors, and community forks such as Trail of Bits’ osql had appeared. On June 18, 2019, a day before the QueryCon conference, the Linux Foundation announced its intent to form a foundation for osquery, with Dactiv, Facebook, Google, Kolide, Trail of Bits and Uptycs participating; the project then had more than 280 contributors and 5,000 commits. Facebook handed over control of funding, infrastructure and code review to a Technical Steering Committee of engineers from Facebook, Trail of Bits, Google and Kolide plus an independent consultant, and the forks were merged back into one osquery.
Since then releases have kept adding tables and event sources; 5.24.0 came out on October 9, 2026.

choices.why: Most engineers already know SQL, and expressing the operating system as tables lets them filter and join data that would otherwise need many separate commands and scripts.
Logging only what changed between runs of a scheduled query keeps the volume sent to central logging small across large fleets.

osqueryd’s logging plugs into an existing log aggregation pipeline, and components such as config and logger plugins can be swapped at runtime, so osquery fits the systems a team already runs instead of bringing its own back end.
